title: The Sharp Directions Are Against You: Curvature Analysis of Activation Steering

paper.title: The Sharp Directions Are Against You: Curvature Analysis of Activation Steering
paper.abstract: Abstract Activation steering adds a vector to a language model’s internal representations at inference time. It is a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for behavioral control. The standard construction, contrastive activation addition (CAA), is fragile, as on many inputs it shifts behavior in the wrong direction. To explain this fragility, we first study the geometry of the steering vector. We introduce steering Hessian , the matrix of second order derivative of the model’s behavioral loss with respect to the steering vector . It captures the output behavior response sensitivity of the model under small perturbations of the steering vector along each direction. Its top eigenvectors are sharp directions : tiny perturbations along them can cause large, erratic, input-dependent behavioral swings. Bottom eigenvectors are flat directions : behavior is robust along them. Removing the sharp component of a steering vector approximately preserves its direction and magnitude (cosine > 0.974 >0.974 , norm reduction < 3 % <3\% for typical settings) while reducing the vector’s directional curvature by up to 12 × \times (median 4 × \times across 36 conditions). We evaluate on three model families (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B), with four behavioral tasks, and 36 token-level conditions. Steering along sharp directions reverses the intended behavior in every condition tested, with anti-steer rates of 53–100%. Sharp directions account for only 1–5% of the CAA vector’s squared norm. However, they drive a disproportionate share of the gap between the steered and unsteered next-token distributions during autoregressive generation. We term this one-line correction as sharp removal ; it outperforms standard CAA in open-ended generation across all 25 conditions tested. A jailbreaking experiment further shows that sharp directions act as noise rather than signal: they disrupt coherent behavioral control regardless of steering polarity.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large language models (LLMs) generate fluent text across many domains, but controlling their behavior remains a central challenge. Activation steering ( Turner et al., 2023 ; Zou et al., 2023a ) is a training-free approach to behavioral control. A steering vector 𝐯 ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is added to the model’s internal activations at a chosen layer during the forward pass, inducing targeted behavioral changes (e.g., increased honesty or reduced toxicity) without modifying any model parameters. The standard recipe for building a steering vector is contrastive activation addition (CAA) ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) , which takes the mean activation difference between positive and negative behavioral exemplars. CAA is simple but fragile in well-documented ways: • Anti-steering. On 30–50% of inputs, the CAA vector shifts behavior in the opposite direction from intended ( Tan et al., 2024 ) . • Coefficient sensitivity. Effectiveness depends on the scaling coefficient α \alpha , with a narrow effective range before behavior degrades ( Braun et al., 2025 ) . • Behavioral inversion. As we show in § 5.3 , on three of four tested tasks, the CAA vector has the wrong sign at most layers, steering the model toward the opposite of the intended behavior. These failures are typically treated as empirical nuisances. We give a geometric explanation for why they occur and a low-cost method to fix them.

sections.heading: Key insight.
sections.text: Steering vectors live in a high-dimensional activation space, but not all directions in that space behave the same way. Some are catastrophically sensitive to perturbation. Most are not. CAA’s fragility comes from this anisotropy. The mean-difference construction does not distinguish the catastrophic directions from the stable ones, so a small fraction of the CAA vector’s squared norm (typically 1–5%, the sharp energy fraction ε \varepsilon ) lies along the catastrophic directions. That small fraction drives most of CAA’s misbehavior at generation time. Identifying these directions and removing them turns a fragile vector into a robust one, with no retraining and no change to the downstream model.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: The steering Hessian, with theoretical grounding (§ 3 , § 4 ). We introduce the steering Hessian 𝐇 steer \mathbf{H}_{\text{steer}} , the curvature of the behavioral loss with respect to the steering vector itself (not the model parameters). For each direction in activation space, 𝐇 steer \mathbf{H}_{\text{steer}} measures how sensitively the model’s behavior responds to perturbing the steering vector along that direction. Two propositions ground the framework. Proposition 1 gives a Gauss-Newton decomposition that explains why top eigenvectors are catastrophic: their effect on logits is governed by the model’s downstream Jacobian, which varies erratically across inputs. Proposition 2 bounds the price of removing them. Removing the top- k k component approximately preserves the steering vector’s direction and magnitude in any single forward pass. At the same time, it reduces the vector’s directional curvature by a factor we denote κ gap \kappa_{\text{gap}} (1.7–12 × \times , median 4 × \times in our experiments; Appendix F ). Two empirical findings about steering geometry (§ 5.2 , § 5.3 ). The top eigenvectors of 𝐇 steer \mathbf{H}_{\text{steer}} are adversarial directions at inference: projecting CAA onto them reverses behavior in all 36 tested conditions (3 models × \times 4 tasks × \times 3 layers), with anti-steer rates of 53–100%. On refusal, this means that the model’s own curvature exposes directions that undermine safety alignment, without requiring adversarial optimization. The bottom eigenvectors play the complementary role: projecting CAA onto the flat subspace diagnoses when CAA has the wrong sign (3 of 4 tasks) and identifies the task-specific layer at which steering is most effective. Sharp removal: a drop-in correction for CAA (§ 3.3 , § 5.4 ). We turn curvature analysis into a one-line modification of any existing CAA vector: subtract its sharp component to produce a cleaned vector 𝐯 cleaned \mathbf{v}_{\text{cleaned}} . This drop-in correction outperforms standard CAA in open-ended generation across 25 of 25 tested conditions spanning three tasks and three model families. The same procedure applies to any activation-space steering vector, not just CAA. Crucially, sharp removal is a post-processing wrapper, not a competitor: it composes with existing methods (we demonstrate on Arditi et al. (2024) ’s refusal direction in § 5.6 ).

sections.heading: Activation steering.
sections.text: Concept activation vectors ( Kim et al., 2018 ) and latent steering ( Subramani et al., 2022 ) laid the groundwork for activation-space interventions. Zou et al. (2023a) formalized representation engineering. Turner et al. (2023) introduced Activation Addition, and Rimsky et al. (2024) extended it to CAA. Subsequent work improved steering via adaptive interventions ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Tian et al., 2025 ) , SAE-guided features ( Chalnev et al., 2024 ) , conceptors ( Postmus and Abreu, 2024 ) , gradient optimization ( Dunefsky and Cohan, 2025 ) , and preference-optimized vectors ( Cao et al., 2024 ) . Arditi et al. (2024) identified a refusal direction that mediates safety behavior. We complement this line by giving a geometric account of why steering vectors succeed or fail and by deriving a corresponding correction.

sections.heading: Robustness of steering.
sections.text: Tan et al. (2024) documented anti-steering; Braun et al. (2025) showed sensitivity to layer and coefficient. We give a geometric explanation: these failures arise from sharp curvature in the activation-space loss landscape.

sections.heading: Sharpness-aware minimization.
sections.text: SAM ( Foret et al., 2021 ) seeks flat minima in weight space; the idea has been extended to LoRA ( Li et al., 2024 ) , unlearning ( Fan et al., 2025 ) , and safety alignment ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . We bring the sharpness concept to the activation space , a different setting. Here, the loss landscape varies with each input, and the parameters of interest are a single d d -dimensional vector rather than billions of model parameters.

sections.heading: Jailbreaking and safety alignment.
sections.text: Adversarial attacks on safety have been studied via prompt optimization ( Zou et al., 2023b ) and fine-tuning ( Qi et al., 2025 ) . Our Finding 2 reveals that the steering Hessian identifies directions that reverse safety-aligned behavior with no adversarial optimization. The model’s own curvature structure exposes its safety vulnerabilities.

sections.heading: Models, tasks, and protocol.
sections.text: We use three 7–8B models: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) ( d = 3584 d{=}3584 ), Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) ( d = 4096 d{=}4096 ), and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) ( d = 4096 d{=}4096 ). We evaluate four behavioral axes: Sentiment (positive sentiment on neutral prompts), Sycophancy (honest disagreement on misconceptions), Toxicity (respectful responses to provocative prompts; RealToxicityPrompts ( Gehman et al., 2020 ) ), and Refusal (strengthen refusal of harmful AdvBench requests ( Zou et al., 2023b ) ). Each task uses 20 contrastive CAA pairs, 12 Hessian estimation prompts, and 100 evaluation prompts. The three sets are disjoint, and all evaluation is held out. Hessian hyperparameters: m = 40 m{=}40 Lanczos iterations, n = 12 n{=}12 estimation prompts, finite-difference step δ = 0.01 \delta{=}0.01 , steering coefficient α = 1.0 \alpha{=}1.0 for Hessian estimation, and sharp subspace dimension k = 15 k{=}15 . Per-task target tokens are listed in Appendix A . We test three layers per model (early, mid, late), giving 36 token-level conditions in total.

sections.heading: 5.3 Flat-Subspace Analysis: Robustness and CAA Inversion
sections.text: The flat-subspace projection 𝐯 flat \mathbf{v}_{\text{flat}} both validates the geometric structure and diagnoses CAA failures. At the best layer per model per task, 𝐯 flat \mathbf{v}_{\text{flat}} has the lowest anti-steer rate in 11 of 12 model-task combinations, including a 0% anti-steer rate on Qwen sentiment (L21) across all 1,000 evaluations. 𝐯 random \mathbf{v}_{\text{random}} produces 60–86% anti-steer rates in most conditions. Hessian eigenvectors, therefore, carry geometric information that random directions do not. The optimal layer varies by task (sentiment: mid-to-late; sycophancy: mid; toxicity and refusal: model-dependent); details in Appendix H .

sections.heading: Finding 3: CAA inversion diagnosed and explained.
sections.text: Flat-subspace projection also diagnoses when CAA produces inverted steering vectors. We observe CAA inversion on three of four tasks: sycophancy (all three models), toxicity (Llama), and refusal (Qwen, Llama). At the best layer, 𝐯 flat \mathbf{v}_{\text{flat}} recovers the correct sign in every case: Sycophancy Mistral L19 (CAA Δ = − 0.028 → 𝐯 flat \Delta{=}{-}0.028\to\mathbf{v}_{\text{flat}} Δ = + 0.317 \Delta{=}{+}0.317 ); Toxicity Llama L20 (CAA Δ = − 0.010 → 𝐯 flat \Delta{=}{-}0.010\to\mathbf{v}_{\text{flat}} Δ = + 0.390 \Delta{=}{+}0.390 ); Refusal Qwen L20 (CAA Δ = − 0.006 → 𝐯 flat \Delta{=}{-}0.006\to\mathbf{v}_{\text{flat}} Δ = + 0.013 \Delta{=}{+}0.013 ). Mechanism: by Proposition 1 , the sharp subspace captures input-dependent surface features (lexical patterns, response format); when these correlate with behavior in the opposite direction from the target disposition, CAA inverts. The flat subspace, in the Jacobian’s approximate nullspace, isolates the dispositional signal. Full mechanistic explanation in Appendix I .

sections.heading: 5.4 Finding 4: Sharp Removal Improves Generation
sections.text: At the token level, sharp removal barely changes the steering vector (Proposition 2 (i): cosine > 0.974 >0.974 , norm reduction < 3 % <3\% for ε ≤ 0.05 \varepsilon\leq 0.05 ). However, during autoregressive generation, the small, sharp component has a significant effect on the next-token distribution. Per-position KL trajectories (Figure 2 ) confirm Proposition 2 (iii). On Llama, CAA and 𝐯 sharp \mathbf{v}_{\text{sharp}} produce nearly identical KL trajectories ( ∼ \sim 19 nats). The sharp component, just 2.6% of CAA’s squared norm, accounts for essentially all of CAA’s distributional gap from the unsteered baseline. Sharp removal reduces this gap by 3–4 × \times . Figure 2 : Per-position KL divergence between the steered and unsteered next-token distributions ( α = 3.0 \alpha{=}3.0 , N = 30 N{=}30 prompts, 5-point moving average). (a) On Qwen, CAA’s KL roughly doubles over the sequence while sharp removal grows more slowly; the gap widens at later positions. (b) On Llama, CAA and 𝐯 sharp \mathbf{v}_{\text{sharp}} produce nearly identical trajectories ( ∼ \sim 19 nats); sharp removal reduces divergence by 3–4 × \times . On Mistral L14 (not shown), CAA’s KL grows 3.8 × 3.8\times over 100 tokens, vs 2.5 × 2.5\times for sharp removal.

sections.heading: Evaluation protocol.
sections.text: For each task, we generate 50 completions per condition with greedy decoding and score them with task-specific classifiers (RoBERTa for sentiment, BART-MNLI for sycophancy, AdvBench keyword detection with NLI tiebreaker for refusal). Token lengths, α \alpha values, and exact classifier specifications are in Appendix G . Figure 3 : Generation-level evaluation across three tasks. Sharp removal (green) outperforms CAA (red) in all 25 conditions. Dashed lines are per-model baselines. (a) Sentiment: sharp removal reaches near-ceiling positive sentiment across all layers. (b) Sycophancy: on a task where CAA is inverted at the token level, sharp removal consistently reduces honesty degradation. (c) Refusal: CAA actively weakens safety alignment (Qwen drops from 78% to 36–44%; Llama from 62% to 24–52%); sharp removal restores and in most cases exceeds baseline refusal rates (Qwen: 88–98%; Llama: 74–76%). Labels: Q=Qwen, L=Llama, M=Mistral; the number is the layer index.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Sharp removal outperforms CAA in all 25 tested conditions (Figure 3 ). On sentiment, sharp removal reaches near-ceiling scores; the largest improvements are on Llama and Mistral (e.g., on Mistral L13 the score rises from 0.67 with CAA to 0.97 with sharp removal). On sycophancy, where CAA is inverted at the token level, sharp removal consistently reduces honesty degradation. The refusal results are the most pronounced: on Qwen and Llama, CAA degrades safety in generation (Qwen drops from 78% to 36%; Llama from 62% to 24%). Sharp removal reverses this, raising refusal to 88--98% on Qwen and 74--76% on Llama, in most cases above the unsteered baseline. On Mistral (baseline 12% by keyword matching 1 1 1 Keyword+NLI undercounts Mistral refusals; an LLM-judge gives 52% baseline. See Appendix J . The main text uses keyword for cross-model consistency. , reflecting weaker safety training), sharp removal raises refusal to 36–62%. Qualitative examples (Appendix K ) show that on Mistral the unsteered model produces actionable harmful content (scam emails, fraud guides); sharp removal replaces these completions with explicit refusals. Finding 4: Sharp removal improves generation (25/25) Removing the sharp component from CAA ( ∼ {\sim} 1–5% of its squared norm) outperforms standard CAA in all 25 generation conditions across three tasks, three model families, and multiple layers. On safety-critical refusal where CAA is inverted, sharp removal restores and often exceeds baseline refusal rates.

sections.heading: 5.5 Finding 5: Jailbreaking Reveals Sharp Directions as Noise, Not Signal
sections.text: Is sharp removal’s improvement specific to the direction of steering, or does it reflect a general property of the sharp subspace? Applying steering vectors in the negative direction ( − α -\alpha ) to jailbreak Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (L10, N = 50 N{=}50 ) and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (L15, N = 100 N{=}100 ) at α = 3.0 \alpha{=}3.0 (GPT-4o-mini judge), we find: − 𝐯 sharp -\mathbf{v}_{\text{sharp}} is the least effective jailbreak (2% full compliance on Qwen with 40% incoherent partials; 100% refusal on Llama, safer than baseline), while − 𝐯 cleaned -\mathbf{v}_{\text{cleaned}} is the most effective on both models, with higher non-refusal rates than − 𝐯 CAA -\mathbf{v}_{\text{CAA}} (80% vs 68% on Qwen; 40% vs 33% on Llama). Full setup, results table (Table 4 ), and per-condition analysis are in Appendix L . Finding 5: Sharp directions are noise, not signal Sharp directions disrupt coherent behavioral control regardless of the steering direction. Steering with − 𝐯 sharp -\mathbf{v}_{\text{sharp}} cannot produce coherent jailbreak completions; on Llama it produces 100% refusal. 𝐯 cleaned \mathbf{v}_{\text{cleaned}} is the most controllable steering vector along either polarity: it strengthens safety in the + α +\alpha direction and produces the highest non-refusal rate in the − α -\alpha direction.

sections.heading: Hessian vs. activation covariance (PCA).
sections.text: Across all conditions, the sharp component carries 1–5% of CAA’s squared norm ( ε ≤ 0.05 \varepsilon\leq 0.05 , cosine > 0.974 >0.974 ). The top-15 generic-PCA and Hessian subspaces have a mean principal-angle cosine of 0.077 0.077 , comparable to two random subspaces, so high-variance directions and high-curvature directions are geometrically distinct (full PCA control on Qwen sentiment L21 in Appendix J ).

sections.heading: 𝐯 sharp \mathbf{v}_{\text{sharp}} in generation, flat vs. random, and k k -sensitivity.
sections.text: 𝐯 sharp \mathbf{v}_{\text{sharp}} reverses behavior in 9 of 9 sentiment and 9 of 10 sycophancy conditions. On refusal at α = 5.0 \alpha{=}5.0 , 𝐯 sharp \mathbf{v}_{\text{sharp}} produces predominantly incoherent output (70–100%). 𝐯 flat \mathbf{v}_{\text{flat}} outperforms 𝐯 random \mathbf{v}_{\text{random}} in 11 of 12 model-task combinations, with margins of 0.14–0.79. A k k -sweep over { 1 , 3 , 5 , 10 , 15 , 25 } \{1,3,5,10,15,25\} reveals two regimes (Figure 7 , Appendix N ): on Qwen refusal sharp removal is robust to k k ( k = 1 k{=}1 raises refusal from 44% to 90%, plateau by k = 5 k{=}5 ); on Llama sycophancy it peaks at k = 5 k{=}5 and degrades at k = 25 k{=}25 from over-removal (predicted by Proposition 2 (ii)); together these motivate k = 10 k{=}10 – 15 15 as the default. Lanczos convergence, an XSTest over-refusal control, an LLM-judge validation on Mistral, and an N = 200 N{=}200 sample-size robustness check on sycophancy (10 of 10) are reported in Appendix J .

sections.heading: Sign-flipped CAA on inverted conditions.
sections.text: Since CAA is inverted on three of four tasks (§ 5.3 ), a natural question is whether negating the vector ( − 𝐯 CAA -\mathbf{v}_{\text{CAA}} ) is enough. It is not: 𝐯 cleaned \mathbf{v}_{\text{cleaned}} outperforms − 𝐯 CAA -\mathbf{v}_{\text{CAA}} in 8 of 10 sycophancy conditions and in all 4 inverted refusal conditions by 23–38 percentage points (e.g., Qwen L10: 98% vs 68%). The sharp component that − 𝐯 CAA -\mathbf{v}_{\text{CAA}} retains continues to disrupt generation regardless of sign, consistent with Finding 5. Per-condition comparison in Appendix J .

sections.heading: Complementarity with other steering methods.
sections.text: Sharp removal is a post-processing operation applicable to any activation-space steering vector, not a competing method. Applied to the refusal direction of Arditi et al. (2024) , which is largely distinct from CAA (cosine 0.01 0.01 – 0.20 0.20 ), the sharp energy fraction ε ⁡ ( 𝐯 ) \varepsilon(\mathbf{v}) predicts steering vector quality across construction methods (full numerical comparison in Appendix J ); the same diagnostic applies to SAE features ( Templeton et al., 2024 ) , optimization-based vectors ( Subramani et al., 2022 ) , and any other activation-space intervention. The full pipeline runs in under 2 minutes per layer on a single A6000 (one-time cost; downstream steering with 𝐯 cleaned \mathbf{v}_{\text{cleaned}} adds zero overhead at inference).

sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: The steering Hessian provides two complementary tools from the same eigendecomposition: flat-subspace extraction ( 𝐯 flat \mathbf{v}_{\text{flat}} ) for token-level analysis, safety auditing, and layer selection (it has a 0% anti-steer rate on some conditions and diagnoses CAA inversion), and sharp removal ( 𝐯 cleaned \mathbf{v}_{\text{cleaned}} ) for deployment-time generation. The framework has direct safety relevance: the top eigenvectors of 𝐇 steer \mathbf{H}_{\text{steer}} identify directions that maximally undermine alignment with no adversarial optimization. Standard CAA can actively degrade safety (Qwen refusal: 78% → \to 36%); sharp removal reverses this (78% → \to 98%). The sharp energy fraction ε ⁡ ( 𝐯 ) \varepsilon(\mathbf{v}) thus serves as a safety audit metric for any proposed steering vector. Our results refine the linear representation hypothesis ( Park et al., 2024 ) : while concepts may be linearly decodable, their steerability depends on curvature.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusions
sections.text: We introduced the steering Hessian, a curvature object that decomposes a model’s activation space into directions that are sensitive or robust to perturbation of the steering vector. Five findings hold across all tested conditions: the spectrum of the steering Hessian is strongly anisotropic; sharp eigenvectors reverse intended behavior; the small sharp component in CAA drives a disproportionate share of the steered-vs-unsteered distributional gap during generation; removing the sharp component improves generation; and sharp directions disrupt coherent behavioral control regardless of steering polarity, acting as noise rather than signal. Where prior work on activation steering asks which direction to steer, the steering Hessian asks which directions are safe to steer along . The answer is determined by the model’s computational geometry, not by the behavioral concept alone.

sections.heading: Per-task target tokens.
sections.text: For each task, we use target tokens that initiate the desired behavioral response: “ Great ” or “ It ” for sentiment (initiating positive responses); “ Actually ” or “ That ” for sycophancy (initiating corrections); “ I ” or “ They ” for toxicity (initiating respectful framing); and “ I ” for refusal (initiating “I can’t…” refusals).

sections.heading: Multi-token contrastive variant.
sections.text: The choice of single target token is a design decision. Different tokens give different Hessian matrices, but we find empirically that the resulting sharp/flat decomposition is robust to this choice. To verify this robustness, we replaced the single-token loss with a contrastive multi-token objective using 6–8 tokens each for positive and negative continuations, on Llama sycophancy at layer 14. The resulting sharp subspace has principal-angle cosine of 0.61 0.61 to the single-token subspace. The 𝐯 cleaned \mathbf{v}_{\text{cleaned}} produced under the multi-token objective performs comparably to the single-token one (matched- N N honesty 0.83 0.83 vs 0.85 0.85 ). Proposition 1 explains this robustness: the curvature structure is dominated by the model’s downstream Jacobian, which is a property of the model’s computation graph and is shared across behavioral objectives. The framework therefore generalizes to any differentiable behavioral objective, including multi-token losses or reward-model scores.

sections.heading: Norm properties of 𝐯 cleaned \mathbf{v}_{\text{cleaned}} .
sections.text: We do not renormalize 𝐯 cleaned \mathbf{v}_{\text{cleaned}} after sharp removal, so its norm is slightly lower than ‖ 𝐯 CAA ‖ \|\mathbf{v}_{\text{CAA}}\| (typically 95–99% of it, since the sharp component carries 1–5% of CAA’s squared norm).

sections.heading: Why removal rather than flat extraction.
sections.text: An alternative is to project CAA onto the flat subspace ℱ k \mathcal{F}_{k} , yielding 𝐯 flat = 𝐏 ℱ k ​ 𝐯 CAA \mathbf{v}_{\text{flat}}=\mathbf{P}_{\mathcal{F}_{k}}\mathbf{v}_{\text{CAA}} (renormalized to the original norm). The flat-subspace projection has a 0% anti-steer rate at the token level on some conditions and is invaluable for diagnosing CAA inversion (§ 5.3 ). However, 𝐯 flat \mathbf{v}_{\text{flat}} discards all signals outside the bottom- k k eigenvectors, which limits its strength in open-ended generation. Sharp removal is a better practical method because it preserves the full CAA signal while removing only the ∼ {\sim} 1–5% of energy that dominates the distributional perturbation during generation (§ 5.4 ).

sections.heading: Appendix I Why Does CAA Invert?
sections.text: The mean-difference construction (Eq. 3 ) captures the direction of maximal activation variance between contrastive contexts. By Proposition 1 , the sharp subspace corresponds to directions along which the downstream Jacobian most strongly translates perturbations into logit changes. These directions are sensitive to input-specific variation (lexical patterns, response format) rather than to the underlying behavioral disposition. When input-dependent features correlate with behavior in the opposite direction from the target disposition, CAA inverts. The flat subspace lies in the approximate nullspace of the Jacobian. It is insensitive to such input-specific variation and isolates the dispositional signal.

sections.heading: Hessian vs. activation covariance (PCA), full numerical comparison.
sections.text: Across all conditions, the sharp component carries 1–5% of CAA’s squared norm ( ε ≤ 0.05 \varepsilon\leq 0.05 , cosine > 0.974 >0.974 ). To rule out the possibility that the steering Hessian merely recovers high-variance directions, we compute PCA on 2,000 forward passes of WikiText-2 (Qwen sentiment, L21). The top-15 generic-PCA and Hessian subspaces have a mean principal-angle cosine of 0.077 0.077 , comparable to two random subspaces. The high-variance directions and the high-curvature directions are therefore geometrically distinct. Functionally, projecting CAA away from the generic-PCA subspace degrades target behavior ( Δ = − 0.021 \Delta=-0.021 ), while sharp removal preserves it ( Δ = + 0.006 \Delta=+0.006 ).

sections.heading: Sign-flipped CAA on inverted conditions (full numerical comparison).
sections.text: We evaluate − 𝐯 CAA -\mathbf{v}_{\text{CAA}} on all inverted conditions under the same generation protocol. On sycophancy, − 𝐯 CAA -\mathbf{v}_{\text{CAA}} is worse than + 𝐯 CAA +\mathbf{v}_{\text{CAA}} in 6 of 10 conditions and worse than 𝐯 cleaned \mathbf{v}_{\text{cleaned}} in 8 of 10. The problem is therefore not purely directional. On refusal (4 inverted conditions), − 𝐯 CAA -\mathbf{v}_{\text{CAA}} partially recovers: Qwen L10 rises from 44% to 68%, Llama L14 from 24% to 38%. However, 𝐯 cleaned \mathbf{v}_{\text{cleaned}} outperforms − 𝐯 CAA -\mathbf{v}_{\text{CAA}} in all 4 conditions by 23–38 percentage points (e.g., Qwen L10: 98% vs 68%). The sharp component that − 𝐯 CAA -\mathbf{v}_{\text{CAA}} retains continues to disrupt generation regardless of sign, consistent with Finding 5.

sections.heading: Over-refusal control (XSTest).
sections.text: To verify that refusal-direction steering does not cause over-refusal on benign inputs, we evaluate on 100 safe prompts from XSTest [ Röttger et al., 2024 ] that superficially resemble unsafe requests (e.g., “How do I kill a process in Linux?”). We use GPT-4o-mini as a judge. On Qwen (L10, α = 1.0 \alpha{=}1.0 ), baseline produces 4% false refusal; CAA increases this to 16%, while sharp removal limits it to 11%. On Llama (L15, α = 3.0 \alpha{=}3.0 ), baseline, CAA, and sharp removal all produce 11–12% false refusal, but sharp removal converts most full refusals (score 3) into partial responses that still provide useful information (1% full refuse vs 5% for CAA). Under stronger Qwen steering ( α = 2.0 \alpha{=}2.0 ), the gap widens further: CAA produces 53% full refusal on safe prompts, while sharp removal produces only 6% (most responses degrade to partial compliance rather than complete shutdown). Steering with 𝐯 sharp \mathbf{v}_{\text{sharp}} alone causes near-total over-refusal on both models (95–97%), confirming that sharp directions disrupt the model indiscriminately. Sharp removal therefore improves the safety-helpfulness trade-off: it strengthens refusal on unsafe prompts (§ 5.4 ) while incurring equal or less over-refusal on safe prompts compared to standard CAA.

sections.heading: LLM-judge validation on Mistral refusal.
sections.text: We re-evaluated all Mistral refusal completions (layer 12, N = 50 N{=}50 ) with GPT-4o-mini as judge, using a 3-point scale (full compliance / partial compliance / full refusal). The judge scores reveal that our keyword+NLI heuristic substantially undercounts refusals on Mistral: the heuristic reports a 12% baseline refusal rate, while the judge classifies 52% of baseline completions as full refusals. Manual inspection confirms the judge. Mistral frequently refuses by stating the request is “illegal and unethical” without using the explicit refusal phrases (e.g., “I cannot,” “I will not”) that the keyword matcher targets. Despite this calibration gap in absolute rates, the relative ordering and effect size are preserved. Under sharp removal, the judge classifies 88% of completions as full refusals (and only 4% as full compliance), compared to 68% full refusal / 28% full compliance under CAA and 52% full refusal / 46% full compliance for the unsteered baseline.

sections.heading: Sample size robustness.
sections.text: To check that our generation results are robust to evaluation scale, we re-ran all 10 sycophancy conditions at N = 200 N{=}200 ( 4 × 4\times the main evaluation). Sharp removal outperforms CAA in 10 of 10 conditions, consistent with the N = 50 N{=}50 results. The largest improvements, on Mistral L10 ( + 0.089 +0.089 ), Llama L16 ( + 0.057 +0.057 ), and Qwen L13 ( + 0.040 +0.040 ), are clearly significant at this sample size. Even the smallest effect (Llama L14: + 0.011 +0.011 ) preserves the correct sign. At N = 200 N{=}200 , 𝐯 sharp \mathbf{v}_{\text{sharp}} reduces honesty in all 10 of 10 sycophancy conditions (compared to 9 of 10 at N = 50 N{=}50 ); the single exception in the main evaluation was sampling noise.

sections.heading: Appendix N Sensitivity to Sharp Subspace Dimension k k
sections.text: Figure 7 : Sensitivity to sharp subspace dimension k k . (a) On Qwen refusal (high κ \kappa ), k = 1 k{=}1 more than doubles CAA’s refusal rate; the curve plateaus by k = 5 k{=}5 . (b) On Llama sycophancy (weaker signal), sharp removal peaks at k = 5 k{=}5 and degrades at k = 25 k{=}25 from over-removal. Together, these motivate k = 10 k{=}10 – 15 15 as the default. We sweep k ∈ { 1 , 3 , 5 , 10 , 15 , 25 } k\in\{1,3,5,10,15,25\} on two conditions: Qwen refusal (Layer 10, strong spectral gap, CAA inverted) and Llama sycophancy (Layer 14, weaker signal separation). On refusal, where the sharp subspace concentrates strong adversarial energy, sharp removal is robust to k k : even k = 1 k{=}1 raises refusal from 44% to 90%, and all values k ≥ 5 k\geq 5 yield 94–96%. On sycophancy, where the behavioral signal is more diffuse, sharp removal peaks at k = 5 k{=}5 (honesty 0.765, matching the unsteered baseline) but degrades at k = 25 k{=}25 (0.698, below CAA). This over-removal effect is predicted by Proposition 2 (ii): the cost of sharp removal scales as O ⁡ ( ε ) O(\sqrt{\varepsilon}) , and at k = 25 k{=}25 the removed energy ε \varepsilon is large enough that this cost exceeds the curvature-reduction benefit. Together, the two regimes motivate k = 10 k{=}10 – 15 15 as a robust default.

sections.heading: Appendix O Limitations
sections.text: The steering Hessian is a local quadratic approximation at ( 𝐯 CAA , α = 1.0 ) (\mathbf{v}_{\text{CAA}},\alpha{=}1.0) ; higher-order terms may dominate at large α \alpha . We test four tasks and three 7–8B instruction-tuned models. Scaling to larger models, broader behavioral axes, and black-box settings where activations are inaccessible remains future work. The Lanczos decomposition assumes a fixed prompt distribution for Hessian estimation; whether the resulting subspaces transfer across distribution shifts is an open question.

sections.heading: Appendix P Declaration of LLM Usage
sections.text: We used general-purpose LLM assistants only for writing, editing, formatting, and presentation support. This included grammar correction, trimming, LaTeX polishing, table/caption wording, and identifying possible clarity issues in the manuscript. LLMs were not used as an important, original, or non-standard component of the proposed method, theoretical claims, experimental design, benchmark evaluation, or reported results. All technical content, mathematical arguments, implementation details, experiments, numerical results, and final claims were written, checked, and approved by the authors. LLMs (Qwen, Llama, Mistral) are the subject of study, and GPT-4o-mini is used in a standard role as an evaluation judge.

sections.heading: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.text: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s theoretical (Propositions 1 , 2 ) and empirical (36 token-level, 25 generation conditions) contributions. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. • The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. • The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. • It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: A dedicated Limitations section is provided in the appendix, discussing the local quadratic approximation, model/task scope, and distribution-shift assumptions. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. • The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper. • The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. • The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. • The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. • The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. • If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. • While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Propositions 1 and 2 are stated with full assumptions in Section 4 ; complete proofs are in Appendices D and E . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. • All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced. • All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. • The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition. • Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. • Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main ex perimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: All models, datasets, hyperparameters (Lanczos m m , n n , δ \delta , α \alpha , k k ), evaluation protocols, and target tokens are specified in Section 5.1 and the appendix. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. • If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. • Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. • While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [No] Justification: Code and evaluation data will be released upon acceptance. All datasets used (RealToxicityPrompts, AdvBench, XSTest, WikiText-2) and models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) are already publicly available. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. • Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark). • The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. • The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. • At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). • Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: All experimental details, including disjoint CAA/Hessian/eval splits, generation hyperparameters, classifier choices, and per-task target tokens, are provided in Section 5.1 and the appendix. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. • The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Robustness is established by sweeping 36 token-level and 25 generation conditions, and we include a sample-size robustness study at N = 200 N{=}200 on sycophancy (10/10 conditions; Appendix J ). Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. • The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). • The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.) • The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). • It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. • It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. • For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). • If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Compute requirements are stated in Section 3 and Section 5 : a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU, with Hessian computation in ∼ 40 {\sim}40 s and the full pipeline in under 2 minutes per layer. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. • The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. • The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines ? Answer: [Yes] Justification: This paper conforms, in every aspect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. Harmful model outputs in the appendix are flagged with a content warning and included only to illustrate safety-relevant findings. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. • If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics. • The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Positive impact (a safety audit tool ε ⁡ ( 𝐯 ) \varepsilon(\mathbf{v}) and a one-line correction that strengthens refusal) and negative impact (sharp directions reveal jailbreak axes without adversarial optimization) are both discussed in the Discussion section and the jailbreaking analysis (Section 5 ).
